question: How can a movement feel continuous when its melodies and colours keep changing hands?
intro: The middle sketch of La Mer breaks orchestral motion into quick exchanges: a figure flashes in one register, changes colour, then slips away. Paul Paray and the Detroit Symphony Orchestra keep its larger surges inside a short, flexible span. Follow the difference between a recurring motion and a tune that stays put.

sections.label: A · Scattered wavelets
sections.mNote: Small figures and changing instrumental colours establish a flexible pulse.

sections.label: B · Wider surges
sections.mNote: Larger rises and releases preserve the flexible pulse.

sections.label: C · Renewed play
sections.mNote: The texture thins and rebuilds toward the largest later swell.

sections.label: Coda · Dissolving motion
sections.mNote: The late crest recedes into the quiet final exchanges.

cues.title: Small sounds, changing hands
cues.text: The opening combines soft wind notes, divided strings and isolated harp and percussion colours. Rather than following one melody uninterrupted, listen for a figure passing from one register or family to another. The movement’s title is Play of the Waves.
cues.evidence: Durand score pp.174–176 (PDF32–34): https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report places the opening well below the later maximum, with early changes at0:12 and0:24. The description covers the opening passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A supple pulse
cues.text: The score asks for a very flexible rhythm. Short accents, held notes and faster figures need not all point to the same beat. Try keeping the underlying pulse while allowing a melody to lean away from it.
cues.evidence: The movement heading is Allegro (dans un rythme très souple), Durand score p.174; Susan Key describes cross-rhythms in this scherzo-like movement: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer. No metrical change is assigned to0:35.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A place between two larger designs
cues.text: This middle sketch occupies the scherzo-like position within La Mer. Its quick exchanges contrast with the first movement’s growth toward a broad arrival and the finale’s more forceful confrontation. Its lightness is a role inside the three-part work, not a lack of structure.
cues.evidence: Susan Key, LA Phil programme note, describes the second movement as the work’s scherzo and the outer movements’ symphonic roles: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer

cues.title: A crest does not stay
cues.text: An early rise has already fallen back. Follow the smaller motions left in its wake instead of treating the quieter space as a stop. The movement repeatedly gathers weight and then disperses it before a stable plateau forms.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level reaches −7.3dB around1:25, then falls to −20.7 at1:35 and −22.2 at1:40. This is the measured broad contour, not a claim about an exact instrumental release.

cues.title: Colour can join the fragments
cues.text: Listen for similarities of rhythm or contour even when the instrument changes. The ear may connect two fragments before it recognises a complete theme. Debussy’s orchestration makes the handover itself part of the movement’s continuity.
cues.evidence: The changing exchanges in Durand score movement II and the LA Phil discussion of fragments and cross-rhythms support this general listening invitation. The report does not independently identify thematic fragments.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A Paris première in 1905
cues.text: La Mer was first performed in Paris on 15 October 1905, with Camille Chevillard conducting the Concerts Lamoureux. The score’s transparent writing and rapid exchanges therefore had to work as practical orchestral parts, not simply as a private image of moving water.
cues.evidence: Première particulars: IMSLP work catalogue https://imslp.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy,_Claude). Scoring and movement order are in the Durand score; no claim about the première’s execution is made.

cues.title: Space before the next build
cues.text: This stretch begins from a reduced level after another swell. Notice how long the movement can stay active without becoming heavy. The later crescendo will stand out because this region has restored some space around the figures.
cues.evidence: Report: level drops sharply between3:10 and3:15, remains relatively low through3:35, then rises toward3:50–3:55. The strong3:14 novelty peak anchors the change of region.

cues.title: A crest is not an ending
cues.text: The movement has more than one substantial surge. Keep listening beyond each crest for what remains in motion underneath or after it. A peak can be a stage in the movement’s course without being its destination.
cues.evidence: Report: a3:50–3:55 crest recedes around4:05, then the level rises again toward4:45–5:05. The cue uses that contour without naming a chord, cadence or instrumental solo.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One mono side of La Mer
cues.text: Mercury placed all three La Mer movements on the second side of MG 50101. The three separate digital tracks here come from that LP transfer; their file boundaries do not imply three different sessions or three independent works.
cues.evidence: Scanned Mercury MG50101 label and IA file list: https://archive.org/details/lp_ibria-la-mer-prelude-to-the-afternoon-of_paul-paray-claude-debussy-detroit-symphony. Side2 lists all three movements in order.

cues.title: The late crest dissolves
cues.text: The largest recorded surge has passed, and the sound quickly loses weight. The close does not imitate the first movement’s broad final declaration. Listen instead for the figures becoming lighter and leaving more room between them.
cues.evidence: Report: the loudest windows cluster at4:45–5:05; level drops to −17.9dB at5:10 and continues lower toward5:40. Durand score pp.216–222 supplies the retreating closing texture.

cues.title: An ending made from disappearance
cues.text: Let the final soft exchanges and resonance finish without expecting another large chord. The movement’s close makes withdrawal audible: its activity gradually becomes too slight to sustain another wave.
cues.evidence: Report: level is −24.2dB at5:40, −27.0 at5:50 and −32.2 at5:55. Durand score p.222 marks the last sounds very soft; no exact final note is timed.

transitions.title: Small exchanges gather a broader crest
transitions.how: The opening’s quick exchanges do not disappear when the sound grows. They are absorbed into a larger swell, then exposed again as the texture thins. Listen for the difference between increasing weight and a genuinely new pace: the flexible pulse remains a common thread through the changing distribution of figures.
transitions.evidence: Report: strong changes at1:10 and1:24; relative level rises to the1:25 crest before falling by1:35. Durand movement II supplies the fragmentary, rhythmically flexible writing;1:24 is a listening landmark, not a claimed bar boundary.

transitions.title: The sound thins before rebuilding
transitions.how: Another swell releases its pressure into a much lighter region. Debussy continues the movement through short exchanges instead of replacing its mobile character with a long contrasting song. The withdrawal makes the next accumulation of weight easier to hear.
transitions.evidence: Report: the3:10 crest falls to −23.0dB at3:15 and −23.7 at3:20, with a strong3:14 novelty peak. The prose describes the large-scale contour, not individual instruments or a harmonic cadence.

transitions.title: The strongest surge leaves a quieter remainder
transitions.how: The late crescendo recedes abruptly in level, but the closing process still contains motion. Small wind, harp and string gestures take over from the fuller texture. Debussy lets them dissolve toward the final soft resonance rather than rebuilding another large crest.
transitions.evidence: Durand score pp.216–222, the closing withdrawal and very soft last page. Report: maximum windows4:45–5:05 followed by the strong5:10 change and sustained decline. The coda is placed approximately.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement II, printed pp.174–222. Selected broad snapshots; the final withdrawal is located by the5:10 and5:40 audio changes. The score allows glockenspiel or celesta; no choice between them is inferred for this recording.

timeline.note: Soft wind chords and isolated harp and percussion notes accompany divided and plucked strings.
The early animated paragraph passes the line between English horn and flute above short string gestures.
Near the later build, winds and strings enlarge the figures with harp and percussion colour.
The closing retreat exposes clarinet and horn lines around harp figures and quieter strings.
The final page leaves soft flute and harp figures, light percussion and sparse string resonance.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
